title: Looking on him, loved him (Mark 10:17–31)
hook: the rich young man asks, Jesus loves him, and he goes away sad

segments.voice: Yesterday, let the children come: Jesus was indignant when they were sent away. Your line was of such is the kingdom. What did you receive without arguing? Today, a grown man who wants to earn it. Day two hundred nineteen.

Jesus is setting out on the road again when a man comes running up and drops to his knees in the dust. Running. Kneeling. This is someone who really wants an answer. He asks straight out: good master, what must I do to receive eternal life? He's done everything right. He's kept the commandments since he was a boy. He's not a villain in this story. He's the kind of person any parish would love to have. What happens next is sad, and it's also tender.
screen: `A MAN RUNS UP AND KNEELS.` → `WHAT MUST I DO?` → `HE'S DONE EVERYTHING RIGHT.`

segments.voice: First, the look. Jesus lists the commandments, and the man says he's kept them all from his youth. Then Mark adds a line. In the Douay-Rheims: "And Jesus looking on him, loved him." Before the hard part, before any test, Jesus looks at him and loves him. Matthew and Luke tell this story too, and neither of them keeps that line. Mark does. Second, the one thing. "One thing is wanting unto thee: go, sell whatsoever thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me." It's the same invitation the fishermen got. Come, follow me. In Mark's order, the love comes first, then the hard words. Third, the face. Mark says his face fell, and he went away sorrowful, "for he had great possessions." Not angry. Sad. He wanted it, and he couldn't let go. And Mark never tells us whether he came back. The sources are silent. By the way, only Matthew calls him young, and only Luke calls him a ruler. The rich young ruler is all three Gospels folded together. Fourth, the camel. Jesus says it's easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom. The disciples are stunned: then who can be saved? He looks at them too, and says: "With men it is impossible; but not with God." Athanasius tells how a young Egyptian named Anthony heard Jesus's words to a rich man read aloud in church, gave his land away, and went into the desert. Catholic teaching treats selling everything as a call some receive, not a rule for all. But in Mark, the look of love comes before any of it.
screen: `JESUS LOOKED AT HIM AND LOVED HIM.` · `ONE THING IS WANTING: COME, FOLLOW.` · `HE WENT AWAY SORROWFUL.` · `IMPOSSIBLE WITH MEN, NOT WITH GOD.` · then, large: `AND JESUS LOOKING ON HIM, LOVED HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give away one thing you're attached to. Start by sitting still and breathing. Imagine being looked at, the way the man was: not inspected, loved. Stay in that for a minute. Then think of one thing you own that you hold a little too tightly. A jacket, a book, a gadget, a sum of money. Not everything. One thing. Picture who might need it. Decide to give it this week. If you pray, you can ask for open hands. The bell holds the time.
Looking on him. The line Mark keeps: Jesus looked at the rich man and loved him, before he asked anything hard. Today's word.
Your line: he loved him first. Today, before you ask anything hard of someone, look at them for a moment and find one thing to love. Day two hundred nineteen.

howItsDone: Catholic religious brothers and sisters take a vow of poverty, following this invitation literally, while lay Catholics are taught to practice detachment and generosity, often through almsgiving, especially in Lent.

only Mark keeps "looking on him, loved him."

fork.setup: you're the rich man. Jesus looks at you with love and says: sell what you have, give to the poor, and come, follow me. what do you do?
options: argue that the commandments are enough.
fork.reveal: he went away sorrowful, "for he had great possessions." Mark never says whether he came back.

original.note: Greek: he loved him, from agapē. only Mark keeps it.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a rich man failing a test.
what it means: Jesus looks at a good man and loves him first. the hard invitation comes from that love.
what a scholar hears: emblepsas autō ēgapēsen auton, found only in Mark; Athanasius's Life of Antony says Anthony heard this Gospel and gave his land away.

notes: Douay-Rheims Mark 10:21, 10:22, 10:27 given from memory; confirm.
'Only Mark keeps looking on him, loved him', 'only Matthew says young (19:20)', 'only Luke says ruler (18:18)': confirm.

Anthony of Egypt: Athanasius says he heard Matthew 19:21 ('If thou wilt be perfect…') read in church around age 18–20; 'around the year 270' is approximate. The script says 'this story'; confirm acceptable given it was Matthew's version.
'Most are not called to sell everything' reflects the Catholic distinction between the evangelical counsels and the universal call to holiness; confirm phrasing.
Script says Mark is silent on whether he came back: true of all the Gospels.

Editor review: cut 'the biggest question there is', 'one of the saddest scenes in the Gospels', the miscount 'five words', the date 'around the year 270' (Athanasius gives none; Anthony heard Matthew's version, so the script now says 'Jesus's words to a rich man'), and the 'most are not called / all are called' preaching; Anthony is now credited to Athanasius.
